extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, math educators, and graduate students interested in mathematical exposition and lecture/notes preparation
extracted.subtask_description: Preparing expository material (lecture notes, expository papers, or video lectures) that explains mathematical proofs and definitions clearly, motivates steps, and conveys how the ideas were discovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total perspicuity; every step motivated and clear
rubrics_metrics.description: "Solving an open exposition problem means explaining a mathematical subject in a way that renders it totally perspicuous. Every step should be motivated and clear." (Timothy Chow, quoted)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for explanations that leave no mysterious jumps: motivate each step, state reasons for choices, avoid unexplained tricks. Anti-pattern: leaving calculations or definitions unexplained and expecting readers to accept them without insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enable students to feel they could have discovered the results
rubrics_metrics.description: "Ideally, students should feel that they could have arrived at the results themselves." (Timothy Chow, quoted)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure exposition so that the reader can follow the thought process and see how natural the steps are; include intermediate heuristics, toy examples, and the lines of reasoning that would lead someone toward the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain where definitions come from / origin of constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why unusual or technical definitions were introduced — e.g. 'Where did Razborov’s definition come from?' — rather than presenting them as ad hoc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the motivating problems, failed attempts, and thought process that lead to the definition. Provide intuition, examples, and show how the definition addresses specific obstacles. Anti-pattern: presenting a definition with only its formal properties and no motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give a plausible account of how a proof could have been discovered
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an account of discovery: "giving a plausible account of how a proof could have been discovered" so readers see the genesis of the ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrate the sequence of guesses, experiments, and simplifications that suggest the proof strategy. Use historical anecdotes or reconstructed heuristics to make the development feel natural instead of miraculous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak solution: justify why each step is reasonable to attempt
rubrics_metrics.description: A "weak" solution explains for each step of the proof "why it is reasonable to expect somebody to come up with it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each step, state the motivating question or constraint that makes trying that step natural. Scoring note: this minimum level explains plausibility without necessarily giving deeper theoretical guarantees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong solution: give better explanations for calculations than 'try it — it works'
rubrics_metrics.description: A "strong" solution supplies explanations for calculations rather than relying on "Try it — it works."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a calculation is used, provide conceptual reasons or heuristics that make the calculation predictable or inevitable. Anti-pattern: presenting lengthy computations with the only comment being that they succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Super-strong solution: provide advance theoretical reasons for calculations' success
rubrics_metrics.description: A "super-strong" solution is one "where you can come up with such an explanation in advance... for each calculation you have good theoretical reasons for being virtually certain that it will do what you want it to do."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give prior theoretical justification or a meta-argument that predicts why the chosen computations or constructions will work. This is the highest standard of exposition: explain both the method and why it must succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the significance/motivation of results to non-experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Include background on "why the problems you have chosen are actually interesting" so readers unfamiliar with the area understand significance (author's reply to a comment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide context linking the specific result to broader problems (e.g., P vs NP motivation for circuit lower bounds), explain implications, and give an accessible statement of why the topic matters. Anti-pattern: diving immediately into technicalities without reminding readers of the motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: High production clarity for video lectures (audio and legibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: For recorded lectures, ensure good audio and an ability to read what the lecturer writes on the board: "Most taped math lectures I have seen suffer from bad audio and an inability to read what the lecturer is writing on the board. These were very well done!" (student comment)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record with clear microphones, high video resolution, and position cameras/lighting so handwritten material is legible. Anti-pattern: low audio/video quality that obscures exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicit feedback and treat early drafts as corrigible
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge drafts may contain mistakes and invite comments/corrections: the posted pdf was "a first draft and not carefully checked, so if anyone has any comments or corrections, then they will be gratefully received."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label draft status, encourage reader input, and iterate on feedback. This improves clarity and catches errors before final publication.
